answer_text:
# BMI (Body Mass Index) Standard

## 📐 What is BMI?

Body Mass Index (BMI) is a value derived from the mass (weight) and height of a person. It is calculated as body mass in kilograms (kg) divided by the square of body height in metres (m²).

**Formula:**
> **BMI = Weight (kg) ÷ Height (m²)**

---

## 📊 Standard BMI Categories for Adults (WHO / CDC)

The major adult BMI classifications are: **Underweight** (under 18.5), **Normal weight** (18.5 to 24.9), **Overweight** (25 to 29.9), and **Obese** (30 or more).

Obesity is further subdivided into three classes:

| Category | BMI Range |
|---|---|
| 🔵 Underweight | Below 18.5 |
| ✅ Normal / Healthy Weight | 18.5 – 24.9 |
| 🟡 Overweight | 25.0 – 29.9 |
| 🟠 Obesity – Class I | 30.0 – 34.9 |
| 🔴 Obesity – Class II | 35.0 – 39.9 |
| 🔴 Obesity – Class III (Severe) | 40.0 and above |

For adults 20 and older, BMI categories are based on a person's BMI regardless of age, sex, or race.

---

## 👶 BMI for Children & Teens (Ages 2–19)

Because children and teens are growing, their BMI values are expressed relative to others of the same sex and age. These values are called BMI-for-age percentiles. Child and teen BMI categories are based on these percentiles, and include underweight, healthy weight, overweight, obesity, and severe obesity.

| Category | Percentile Range |
|---|---|
| Underweight | Below the 5th percentile |
| Healthy Weight | 5th to less than 85th percentile |
| Overweight | 85th to less than 95th percentile |
| Obese | 95th percentile or above |

---

## 🌏 BMI Standards for Asian Populations

The standard WHO categories were developed primarily from European and North American data. Research has shown that the health risks associated with specific BMI values differ across ethnic groups. In 2004, a WHO expert consultation recommended that Asian countries consider using lower cutoff points (23 for overweight, 27.5 for obesity).

| Category | Standard BMI | Asian BMI |
|---|---|---|
| Overweight | ≥ 25.0 | ≥ 23.0 |
| Obese | ≥ 30.0 | ≥ 27.5 |

---

## ⚠️ Health Risks Associated with BMI

Higher BMI levels have been linked to multiple diseases, such as **heart disease, arthritis, Type 2 diabetes mellitus, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and certain cancers**.

There is an increased risk of obesity-related diseases, health conditions, and mortality associated with a BMI greater than 30. Conversely, there is an associated risk of mortality with a BMI less than 18.5.

---

## ⚕️ Limitations of BMI

Although BMI is a widely used and useful indicator of healthy body weight, it does have its limitations. BMI is only an estimate that cannot take body composition into account. Due to a wide variety of body types as well as distribution of muscle, bone mass, and fat, BMI should be considered along with other measurements rather than being used as the sole method for determining a person's healthy body weight.

Bodybuilders or other very muscular people can have a high BMI because of their muscle mass, even though they're not necessarily in the overweight range. BMI can also underestimate body fat in people who have lost muscle mass, such as some older people.

> 💡 **Tip:** Always consult a healthcare provider for a complete health assessment, as BMI is just one of many tools used to evaluate overall health.
